title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance guidance for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, the secure software development lifecycle (Secure SDLC), incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and management of risk & exceptions. It is intended for engineering, security, product, and audit stakeholders responsible for implementing or assessing controls.

Scope
Applies to all Redwood services, control planes, customer-facing APIs, deployment configurations (hosted, dedicated, private), developer tooling, and associated CI/CD pipelines.

Owners and contacts
- Document owner: Security Team (security@redwood.ai)
- Primary author: Aisha Patel (Security Engineering)
- Reviewers: Carlos Mendes (Platform Security), Emily Zhao (Compliance), Marta Ruiz (Privacy)
- Escalation contact: oncall-security@redwood.ai

1) RBAC & Authentication

Summary
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) enforces least privilege across Redwood resources (console, control plane APIs, infra accounts, internal tooling). Authentication is provided via SSO (OIDC) and service identity (short-lived mTLS or SPIFFE identities for services).

Goals
- Enforce least privilege by default.
- Provide auditable role assignment and periodic access reviews.
- Support separation of duties for sensitive operations (key rotation, production rollout, incident remediation).

Roles and privileges (high level)
- org:owner — full org-level configuration, billing, and policy controls (restricted to executive ops).
- security-admin — manage security config, exceptions, and controlbook updates.
- infra-admin — manage cloud accounts, VPC, and fleet-level infrastructure (requires approval for production changes).
- svc-deployer — deploy application-level changes to staging & production via CI with approval gates.
- dev / viewer — read-only access to non-sensitive dashboards and docs.

Authentication flows
- Human users: SSO (Okta) with enforced MFA (hardware token or TOTP fallback).
- Service-to-service: short-lived mTLS with SPIFFE IDs, rotated via automated CA (managed by infra).
- CI identities: ephemeral tokens issued by CI (GitHub Actions/GitLab) with constrained scopes; personal long-lived tokens are prohibited for CI.

Access lifecycle & reviews
1. Onboarding: role assignment via HR ticket + manager approval; approvals recorded in IAM ticket system.
2. Periodic review: quarterly access review owned by Security (reviewers: team leads).
3. Offboarding: account disablement within 2 business days of termination; emergency revocation via IAM revoke runbook.

Enforcement controls and SLOs
- All privileged mutations require just-in-time approval for org:owner and infra-admin roles.
- 100% of privileged role assignments must have a linked JIRA ticket for auditability.
- Quarterly reviews completed within SLA: 95% of accounts reviewed within 7 days of quarterly window.

2) Audit Logging

Principles
- Immutable, tamper-evident logs for authentication, authorization decisions, admin actions, model onboarding, and data movement events.
- Central collection and retention policy aligned to data residency and compliance needs.

What we log (minimum)
- Auth events: login success/failure, MFA success/failure, token issuance/refresh, SSO provisioning actions.
- Authorization checks: policy evaluations, resource access denials, role changes.
- Admin activities: deployments, infrastructure changes, key rotations, config modifications.
- Data events: data ingress/egress, export requests, customer-tier exports.

Log collection and pipeline
- Agents (Fluentd) stream structured JSON logs to the central logging cluster (encrypted in transit).
- Logs are ingested into a write-once storage (S3 with object lock or equivalent) and indexed for query in the SIEM (Splunk/Elastic).
- Integrity: periodic snapshot hashes are recorded in an audit index; critical logs have cryptographic signatures.

Retention and access
- Standard retention: 1 year for operational logs.
- Extended retention: 7 years for security-sensitive logs (authz changes, admin actions) for customers with contractual requirements.
- Access to raw logs is controlled by RBAC and requires justifiable ticketing; read access to the SIEM is logged and reviewed monthly.

Alerting and monitoring
- Define high-fidelity alerts for anomalous auth patterns (immediate), privilege escalations (P0), and data exfiltration patterns (P0).
- Alert SLO: 90% of security alerts acknowledged within 15 minutes during business hours.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Policy overview
- Data residency choices (region selection) are supported for customer deployments (hosted region, dedicated region, private VPC).
- Residency guarantees are documented in customer contracts and enforced through routing and storage controls.

Data classification and mapping
- Classify datasets: public, internal, confidential, regulated (PII/PHI/financial).
- Mapping table (example, described in text):
  - public: telemetry aggregates — allowed in any region.
  - internal: product configs — retained in primary region with 30d backup copy in DR region.
  - confidential: customer prompts & fine-tuning data — stored only in customer-selected region; encryption with customer-managed keys optional.
  - regulated: PII/PHI — stored and processed only in approved regions and subject to retention rules below.

Retention rules (examples)
- Operational telemetry: 90 days hot, 1 year warm, delete after 3 years.
- Auth and access logs: 1 year standard, extendable to 7 years per contract.
- Customer content (raw prompts): retention determined by customer setting; default 30 days unless contract specifies longer.
- Backups: encrypted snapshots retained for 90 days by default; longer retention per contract.

Enforcement mechanisms
- Storage policies at object-store level (lifecycle policies), encryption at rest by default, and region-scoped buckets.
- Automated compliance checks run weekly to detect off-region objects; failing objects are quarantined and ticketed.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Software Development Lifecycle)

Goals
- Integrate security early and throughout the development lifecycle.
- Ensure all code and infra changes meet baseline security checks before reaching production.

Phases and controls
- Design: Threat modeling required for any service or feature interacting with customer data or auth. Owner: feature/product lead + security reviewer.
- Implementation: Code must meet static analysis checks (SAST), dependency scanning (Software Composition Analysis), and linting.
- Build/CI: Pipelines run unit tests, integration tests, SCA, and policy checks. Only signed CI artifacts may be promoted.
- Release: Production rollout requires automated preflight checks (canary metrics, perf guardrails) and an approval from a designated approver for infra or data-impacting changes.
- Post-release: Automated telemetry and regression detection (security & quality) for 48 hours after release.

Required tooling and gating
- CI gating: All PRs require 2-engineer reviews and green CI. Security-critical PRs require security reviewer approval.
- Secret scanning: Block merges when high-risk secrets are detected.
- Dependency policy: High/critical CVEs in transitive dependencies must be addressed within 7 days or accompanied by approved risk exception.

Developer training and metrics
- Mandatory annual Secure SDLC training for engineers.
- Metric: % of releases with completed threat model (target 95%).

5) Incident Response: Security Procedures

Objective
Provide clear, reproducible procedures for security incidents affecting confidentiality, integrity, and availability of Redwood services and customer data.

Incident categories and severity
- Sev 1 (P0): Active data exfiltration, production-wide outage caused by security compromise.
- Sev 2 (P1): Targeted compromise, privilege escalation without confirmed exfiltration.
- Sev 3 (P2): Vulnerability discovered with limited blast radius.

Playbook (high level)
1. Detection & Triage: Security on-call acknowledges within 15 minutes; triage to classify severity and impact.
2. Containment: Apply temporary network rules, revoke tokens, and isolate affected services; document all actions in the incident log.
3. Eradication & Recovery: Patch or remove malicious artifacts, restore from clean snapshots, and validate integrity.
4. Post-incident review: Conduct blameless postmortem within 5 business days for Sev1/Sev2; include timelines, root cause, and action items.

Security-specific steps
- Evidence preservation: Preserve immutable copies of affected logs and system snapshots. Use object-lock or write-once storage for critical evidence.
- Forensic activities: All forensic access requires approval from the incident commander and must be logged.
- Customer notification: Follow contractual SLAs; for P0 incidents, initial notification to impacted customers within 24 hours. Legal and privacy teams coordinate external communication.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose
Standardize how evidence for audits (SOC2, ISO27001, GDPR controls) is generated, stored, and reviewed.

Evidence types and owners (textual table)
- Control: RBAC assignments — Evidence: IAM export + approval tickets — Owner: Security.
- Control: Log retention and integrity — Evidence: Retention policy docs + signed log snapshots — Owner: Eng-Infra / Security.
- Control: Secure SDLC — Evidence: CI run history, SCA reports, threat models — Owner: Eng-DevEx + Security.

Workflow steps
1. Evidence collection: Automated exports where possible (IAM reports, SIEM exports, pipeline artifacts).
2. Evidence tagging: Each artifact is tagged with control ID, date, and reviewer in the evidence repository.
3. Review & sign-off: Security and Compliance reviewers validate evidence; a signed attestation is stored.
4. Audit delivery: Curated evidence bundles are prepared for external auditors; privileged access is granted on a per-audit basis and logged.

Retention and archival
- Audit artifacts: retain for a minimum of 3 years or per auditor request.
- Evidence repository access: limited to compliance and security reviewers; all access is logged.

7) Risk & Exceptions

Risk exception policy
- Exceptions are temporary, time-boxed, and must include mitigations and a clear owner.
- Exception request form fields (text): control impacted, justification, compensating controls, proposed end date, risk owner, reviewer approvals.

Exception lifecycle
1. Request submission: Requestor submits form and links evidence.
2. Review: Security evaluates risk; business impact reviewed by Product/Legal if needed.
3. Approval: For high-risk exceptions, Exec-sponsor required. Approvals are stored in the exception registry.
4. Remediation tracking: Exceptions tracked in quarterly roadmap; renewals require re-approval.

Metrics and guardrails
- Max active exceptions: measured monthly; target: <5 high-risk exceptions active at any time.
- Exception duration: default max 90 days; renewals require additional justification.

Appendices
A. Quick runbooks (links and CLI examples)
- Revoke access immediately: "./scripts/iam-revoke --user <username> --reason 'offboard'"
- Export auth logs for incident: "./tools/log-export --start 2026-02-01T00:00Z --end 2026-02-10T00:00Z --filter 'user:alice' --output /tmp/evidence.zip"
- Quarantine off-region object: "python tools/quarantine_offregion.py --bucket my-bucket --region us-east-1"

B. Example evidence export checklist (text)
- IAM role export CSV, linked JIRA ticket IDs for each privileged assignment, signed attestation from manager, SIEM export for relevant timeframe, CI artifact hashes, encrypted backup manifest.
